lab.guided.payments.basis: Payment ÷ GMV in a month, as a percentage. Each figure is computed TWICE: first within one simulated path, over that path's ACTIVE months only — months with positive revenue and a positive payment — and then averaged across the 500 paths. So the peak is the average of each path's own worst month, not one worst month across the cohort, and the 90th percentile is the average of path-level 90th percentiles, not a pooled percentile. There is no monthly series behind these figures. Months with zero revenue, and months after the contract completes, are excluded rather than counted as zero burden.

labpage.caveat.0: Every figure here is simulation output under stated assumptions. No observed seller revenue, repayment or default outcome exists in this project.
labpage.caveat.1: The fixed arms are modelled as paid in full and on time in every month of the schedule. The fixed arm is therefore an OPTIMISTIC SCHEDULED-RECOVERY BENCHMARK: it shows what the schedule would deliver under that assumption. It is not an upper bound derived from anything measured here, and this project makes no claim about how often real fixed-payment borrowers miss payments.
labpage.caveat.2: Whether revenue-based repayment recovers faster or slower depends on the revenue path, and both directions appear in this scenario library. Nothing here supports a universal claim in either direction.
labpage.caveat.3: Intervals in the underlying artifacts are Monte Carlo intervals over simulated paths. They are not population confidence intervals and say nothing about real sellers.
labpage.caveat.4: {grid} The label describes how the price was chosen, not an outcome guaranteed on any path: across simulated paths the realised rate differs again, because duration varies with revenue and a longer duration lowers the annualised rate for the same total.
labpage.caveat.5: Mean duration and mean rate have DIFFERENT denominators and must be read separately. Mean duration covers only paths that reached the repayment target. Mean rate covers paths with a defined internal rate of return — a larger set, because an incomplete path that made payments still has a rate over the observed window. Neither is automatically a portfolio-wide outcome; each describes the subset it was computed over, and both should be read beside the incomplete-recovery rate.
labpage.caveat.6: Payment burden is measured against revenue, not against what the seller retains. Margins, operating costs, reserves and other debts are outside the model, so a lower burden is not by itself evidence that a contract is affordable.
labpage.finding.burdenDenominator: Contractual remittance is a fixed share of NET SALES, so the contractual burden is constant by construction. The burden shown here uses a different denominator — payment ÷ GMV — so it equals r·(1 − return rate) and MOVES when the return rate moves. It is constant only in scenarios where the net-sales/GMV ratio is fixed. Most registered scenarios hold that ratio fixed; `returns_spike` is the explicit exception where the displayed burden moves.
labpage.finding.completionDiffers: Completion is reported separately and differs between them: {eqPct} of the cost-matched arm's paths and {illPct} of the illustrative arm's reached the repayment target.
labpage.finding.completionSame: Completion is reported separately: {eqPct} of paths reached the repayment target under both.
labpage.finding.contractualVsDisplayed: A revenue share makes the CONTRACTUAL remittance a fixed share of net sales, so the contractual burden does not rise when revenue falls. The burden displayed here uses a different denominator — payment ÷ GMV — so it is constant only while the net-sales/GMV ratio is fixed, and it varies when returns vary. The price of the revenue-contingent structure is a MORE VARIABLE recovery period whose direction depends on the realised path: under P4 revenue-contingent recovery leads a cost-matched fixed schedule when the realised mean eligible base clears B* = P/r and lags when it does not, and both occur in the registered scenarios. Calling it uniformly longer would state one scenario's direction as a property of the structure. Which side of that trade is worth taking is a commercial judgement this study does not make.
labpage.finding.fixedBurdenInverse: A fixed instalment does not adjust, so its burden rises in INVERSE proportion to revenue: halve revenue and the burden doubles. (It does not rise 'in proportion' — that would mean falling with revenue, which is what the revenue share does.) Under a revenue share the expected repayment period lengthens instead. That is a statement about the payment rule, not about whether the contract is ultimately repaid: where revenue stops before the cap is reached, a balance goes unrecovered. The trade is timing, not forgiveness — and not immunity.
labpage.finding.incompleteRecovery: In the {scenario} scenario {pct} of simulated paths do not reach the repayment target within the 24-month window. That is censoring under this scenario's revenue path, not a modelled default.
labpage.finding.notComparableOnRate: In the {scenario} scenario these two revenue-based arms cannot be compared on rate alone. The cost-matched arm shows {eqRate}, averaged over the {eqDefined} of its paths with a defined rate; the illustrative arm shows {illRate} over {illDefined} of its paths. Those are differently selected sets, so the difference between them combines price with selection.
labpage.finding.openQuestion: Whether real sellers would repay on these paths, and at what default rate, cannot be answered here. It needs observed revenue and adjudicated repayment outcomes.
labpage.finding.peakBurden: In the {scenario} scenario, the cost-matched fixed arm reaches a peak payment burden of {fixedPct}, against {rbfPct} for the revenue-based arm.
labpage.finding.priceStructureSeparable: Price and structure are separable. The same revenue-share structure priced at the reference-path cost-matched factor shows a mean simulated rate of {eqRate} in the {scenario} scenario, against {illRate} at the illustrative 1.20 factor. Both means are taken over the same share of paths — {definedPct} have a defined rate under each — so the rate comparison is like-for-like and the difference is a property of the chosen cap factor, not of revenue-based repayment.
labpage.finding.ratesEqual: Both cap factors give the same mean simulated rate of {rbfRate} in the {scenario} scenario. Neither cap binds before revenue stops, so the two contracts make identical payments and their observed-window rates coincide despite different contractual targets.
labpage.finding.recovery12: In the {scenario} scenario, recovery by month 12 reaches {fixedPct} of target for {fixedArm} and {rbfPct} of target for {rbfArm} — so {fixedArm} is {direction} {rbfArm} here. The two targets differ, so this is not a comparison of amounts recovered.
labpage.finding.recovery12SameTarget: In the {scenario} scenario, recovery by month 12 reaches {fixedPct} of target for {fixedArm} and {rbfPct} of target for {rbfArm} — so {fixedArm} is {direction} {rbfArm} here. Both target {target}, so these percentages compare like for like.
labpage.finding.underreportingOwed: Under-reporting does not change what is owed. It rescales the UNCAPPED remittances — the final payment is clipped to whatever is left, so it does not scale with ω — and raises the cumulative sales needed to reach the cap. Invariance of the total is conditional on the cap actually being reached: under-reporting severe enough to push the contract past the horizon leaves the cap unreached and the total short.
labpage.finding.underreportingSweepCompl: In this sweep every path still reached the cap inside the 24-month window, so the total stayed at the cap and only the duration moved: {fromMonths} → {toMonths} months as ω falls {fromOmega} → {toOmega}. That is this sweep's result, not a general guarantee.
labpage.finding.underreportingSweepIncom: In this sweep some paths did NOT reach the cap inside the 24-month window, so the total is not invariant across all of them — read the incomplete-recovery column.
labpage.finding.windowNote: Where the repayment target is not reached, the rate is an observed-window figure over the 24-month horizon, not the cost of a repaid contract.
labpage.glossary.0.text: The multiple of the advance that the seller repays in total. A cap factor of 1.20 on a 100M advance means 120M repaid.
labpage.glossary.1.text: The total amount repayable — advance × cap factor. Collection stops when it is reached.
labpage.glossary.2.text: The share of each month's revenue that goes to the financier. Fixed as a percentage; the amount moves with revenue.
labpage.glossary.3.text: The annualised internal rate of return of the payment stream against the advance. It puts a revenue share and a fixed instalment on one axis.
labpage.glossary.4.text: Payment ÷ GMV in a given month — the share of that month's gross takings that leaves as a payment. The contract charges its share on NET sales, so this equals r·(1 − return rate) and varies when returns vary.
labpage.glossary.5.text: The value exceeded in only 10% of active months. It describes a bad month, not a typical one.
labpage.glossary.6.text: A range showing whether enough simulated paths were run for a number to be stable. It is NOT a confidence interval and says nothing about real sellers.
labpage.glossary.7.text: A committed, checksummed result file. Identical code, configuration and seeds reproduce it byte-for-byte within a fixed runtime, and numerically at published precision on every platform tested — so any figure here can be traced to a verifiable file.
labpage.glossary.8.text: A flat, shock-free revenue path used once to price the fixed benchmark. Contracts are priced at origination, so a later shock cannot retro-price them.
labpage.grid.exact: The cost-matched cap factor is the nearest point found on the registered 0.0005-step search grid. On this sweep that point lands on the benchmark's {benchmark} to displayed precision.
labpage.grid.residual: The cost-matched cap factor is the NEAREST POINT FOUND ON THE REGISTERED 0.0005-step search grid: it prices at {achieved} against the amortizing loan's {benchmark}, a residual of about {residual} percentage points. That residual is a GRID-RESOLUTION result — it reflects how finely the search was stepped, not a limit on what is attainable. Within an interval where the paying-month count stays fixed, the clipped final payment changes continuously with the cap factor, so the effective APR does too; a numerical root exists on the reference path at approximately f = {rootF}. Changes in the paying-month count create kinks in that relationship, not gaps.
labpage.grid.unavailable: The cost-matched cap factor is the nearest point found on the registered search grid, not a solved root; the pricing artifact needed to quote the residual is not loaded.
labpage.metric.burden.caveat: Burden is measured against REVENUE, not against what the seller has left. Margins, operating costs, reserves and other debts are not modelled, so a lower burden here does not establish that a contract is affordable.
labpage.metric.burden.definition: Payment ÷ GMV in a given month — note the denominator is GMV while remittance is charged on net sales, so this is r·(1 − return rate), not r. Computed from revenue alone; undefined in months with zero revenue.
labpage.metric.burden.why: It is the share of this month's takings that leaves as a payment.
labpage.metric.duration_months_mean.cave: Where any path fails to complete, this is a SURVIVOR statistic. It describes the contracts that finished, not the portfolio. A scenario with a short mean duration and a high incomplete-recovery rate is not a fast contract — it is one where the slow paths were dropped rather than counted.
labpage.metric.duration_months_mean.defi: Mean months until cumulative payments reach the repayment target — computed ONLY over paths that reached it within the 24-month window. Paths that did not are excluded from this mean and reported separately as incomplete recovery.
labpage.metric.duration_months_mean.why: Revenue-based repayment extends the term when revenue falls, rather than holding the payment fixed. In the scenarios where the term extends, that extension is the provider's cost. Extension is NOT the same as preventing default: where revenue stops PERMANENTLY BEFORE COMPLETION while a contractual balance remains, no further payment occurs and the cap is never reached. A temporary zero-revenue spell is a different case and usually still completes -- temp_closure leaves 2.0% of paths incomplete at f = 1.20 and none at f*. Read this beside the incomplete-recovery rate.
labpage.metric.effective_apr.caveat: Read the two denominators separately. DURATION is averaged over completing paths only. THIS RATE is averaged over paths with a defined internal rate of return, which is a different and usually larger set — an incomplete path that made payments has a defined rate over the OBSERVED WINDOW, and that is a window figure, not a final lifetime return. Neither conditional mean is automatically a portfolio-wide outcome: each describes the subset it is computed over, so read both beside the incomplete-recovery rate rather than treating either as the scenario's result. Paths that fall short are not 'unprofitable' — profitability is computed nowhere in this project; they simply did not reach the cap inside the horizon. Separately, this is the MEAN ACROSS SIMULATED PATHS, not the reference-path rate the cost-matched contract was priced on.
labpage.metric.effective_apr.definition: Annualised internal rate of return of the payment stream against the advance, averaged over the paths where a rate EXISTS. Existence is the only condition: the mean is NOT restricted to paths that reached the repayment target. A path that stopped short of the cap but made payments still has a well-defined rate over the observed window, and it is counted here. Only a path that repays nothing at all has no rate and is excluded.
labpage.metric.effective_apr.why: Puts a revenue share and a fixed instalment on one axis.
labpage.metric.high_burden_months.caveat: These thresholds are ILLUSTRATIVE reporting bands chosen for this study. They are not validated hardship cutoffs and no claim is made that crossing one causes distress. For a revenue share the count is constant in these scenarios, but NOT by construction: the remittance is a fixed share of net sales while this count is measured against payment ÷ GMV, so it can move when the return rate moves. It is constant only while the net-sales/GMV ratio holds fixed. The informative side is the fixed arm.
labpage.metric.high_burden_months.defini: Count of months where payment burden exceeds 10%, 15%, 20% or 25%, out of a 24-month window.
labpage.metric.high_burden_months.why: Averages hide bad months. This counts them.
This is NOT a default rate. No borrower behaviour and no default is simulated on any arm.
Share of simulated paths that do not reach the repayment target within the 24-month observation window.
labpage.metric.recovery_ratio.caveat: Denominators differ by arm, so read each arm against its own target rather than comparing absolute amounts recovered.
labpage.metric.recovery_ratio.definition: Share of the arm's own repayment target recovered by month 12, 18 and 24. For the revenue-based and cost-matched fixed arms the denominator is the contractual cap; for the amortizing loan, which has no cap, it is scheduled total repayment.
labpage.metric.recovery_ratio.why: The other side of the trade-off. Where recovery is slower it is a real cost to the financier even when the full amount is eventually repaid — but the direction is not universal. Revenue-contingent recovery may lead or lag the cost-matched fixed arm depending on the realised path (P4), and both occur in the registered scenarios. Read the direction per scenario.

labpage.taxonomy.mathematical_property.m: Holds for any revenue path, by proof. Independent of the simulation, the parameters, and any distributional assumption. See research/DERIVATIONS.md.
labpage.taxonomy.open_real_world_questio: Cannot be settled by this project. Requires observed seller revenue and adjudicated repayment outcomes, which do not exist here.
labpage.taxonomy.product_implication.mea: A design consequence the author draws from the above. A judgement, not a measurement.
labpage.taxonomy.sensitivity_result.mean: How an output moves when a parameter is swept. Shows what the conclusion depends on, not that the parameter is right.
labpage.taxonomy.simulation_result.label: Simulation result
labpage.taxonomy.simulation_result.meani: Measured on simulated revenue paths under the frozen methodology, FOR THE SELECTED SCENARIO. Describes the model, not observed sellers, and does not generalise to other scenarios.
labpage.under.whyNotScenario: This is a parameter sweep, not a revenue path. ω is the share of true revenue the provider observes; the underlying revenue shape is held fixed. It is shown separately so it is not read as one of the scenarios.

questions.a1: No. RBF holds no capital, makes no credit offers and is not a lending service. It is independent research and a software demonstration.
questions.a2: No. It examines contractual mechanics under specified revenue scenarios. It does not establish creditworthiness, predict default or assess suitability for a particular merchant.
questions.a3: No. Vietnamese e-commerce motivates the research, but the scenario parameters are modelling assumptions, not estimates from a representative seller dataset.
questions.a4: Not here. There is no historical-record upload on this website. Use synthetic examples only in the prototype; its submission flow can store records and send administrator notifications.
